title: 1960: Sharpeville and the Armed Struggle
summary: The formation of the PAC, the Sharpeville massacre of 21 March 1960, the banning of the liberation movements, the turn to armed struggle and the Rivonia Trial.

notes.text: In **1959** some members left the ANC to form the **Pan Africanist Congress (PAC)**, led by **Robert Sobukwe**. The PAC believed that Africans should lead their own liberation and disagreed with the multiracial Congress Alliance and parts of the Freedom Charter.

The PAC called on people to leave their passes at home and present themselves for arrest at police stations, so that the jails would be overwhelmed. At **Sharpeville**, near Vereeniging, about 5 000 to 7 000 unarmed people gathered outside the police station. The police opened fire: **69 people were killed** and about 180 wounded. Most were shot in the back while running away.

notes.title: Source I: A survivor's account (a composite based on survivors' testimonies)
notes.text: We were singing and some were laughing. Nobody had a weapon. Then the shooting started and people began to fall. We ran, but the bullets were following us. I saw a woman fall next to me; she was shot in the back.

notes.title: Source J: A police commander's view (a composite based on police statements to the press in 1960)
notes.text: The native mentality does not allow them to gather for a peaceful demonstration. For them to gather means violence. My men were in danger and had to defend themselves.

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: When two sources disagree, consider who wrote each one and why. The police commander had a reason to justify the shooting; his words also show racist assumptions. Evidence of wounds in the back supports the survivors' account.

notes.title: What happened and why it mattered
notes.problem: Summarise Sharpeville in three steps: cause, event and result.
steps: Cause: the PAC called on people to protest against pass laws by going to police stations without passes.
Event: police fired on the crowd, killing 69 people.
Result: a state of emergency, the banning of the ANC and PAC, and world condemnation.
notes.answer: A peaceful protest ended in a massacre that changed the struggle.

items: There was worldwide condemnation; for the first time, the UN Security Council criticised South Africa.
A **State of Emergency** was declared and about 18 000 people were detained.
On **8 April 1960** the **ANC and PAC were banned** under the Unlawful Organisations Act.
In 1961 South Africa became a **republic** and left the Commonwealth.
Peaceful protest seemed impossible, so the movements turned to **armed struggle**.
21 March is now **Human Rights Day** in South Africa.

notes.caption: From peaceful protest to armed struggle: the turning points of the early 1960s.

notes.text: In **1961** the ANC and the South African Communist Party formed **Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK)**, 'Spear of the Nation', with Mandela as its first commander. MK began a campaign of **sabotage** on 16 December 1961, attacking government buildings, power lines and railways while trying to avoid loss of life. The PAC's armed wing was called **Poqo** (later APLA).

notes.title: Why turn to armed struggle?
notes.problem: Why did the ANC form Umkhonto we Sizwe in 1961?
steps: Decades of peaceful protest had brought harsher laws.
After Sharpeville, the ANC and PAC were banned, so legal protest was impossible.
The leaders decided that sabotage of state targets was the next step.
notes.answer: Peaceful means had been shut down.

notes.text: In July 1963 police raided **Liliesleaf Farm** in Rivonia, the secret headquarters of MK, and arrested Walter Sisulu, Govan Mbeki, Ahmed Kathrada and others. Mandela, already in prison, was tried with them for sabotage. In **June 1964**, eight of the accused, including Mandela, were sentenced to **life imprisonment**, most of them on **Robben Island**.

notes.title: Source K: From Nelson Mandela's statement at the Rivonia Trial, 20 April 1964
notes.text: I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination. I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities. It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.
Through the 1960s the government crushed internal resistance. Leaders were jailed, banned or forced into **exile**; Oliver Tambo led the ANC from abroad, building international support.
